title: How can local weather knowledge be integrated within climate adaptation services?
subtitle: Designing across knowledge systems for resilient agricultural decision-making in rural Ghana

table.topic: Case study of the DROP climate service app and its relationship with local weather knowledge and community practices in Ghana

intro: Designing across knowledge systems for resilient agricultural decision-making in rural Ghana.

body.heading: Research Gap
body.text: In recent years, the emphasis on local knowledge integration within climate services for climate adaptation has grown. However, research on its practical implementation remains limited. Further, climate services have been primarily investigated from a technical perspective without accounting for the social and cultural impacts on communities and knowledge practices.

body.heading: Objective & Use Case
body.text: This thesis analyzes the representation and transformation of local knowledge and community dynamics through the case of the DROP app, a climate service used by smallholder farmers in Ghana. The analysis focuses on its current design and deployment in the country where the app was initially developed, and examines how it integrates scientific and local knowledge into digital climate service tools.

body.heading: Framework & Methodology
body.text: The research is grounded in service design and design research lenses, including multi-level service design, systems thinking, and the concept of soft impacts of technological innovation. It adopts a qualitative, exploratory, participatory methodology with community-based fieldwork in Ghana.

body.heading: Findings
body.text: Findings illustrate local knowledge as highly localized, nuanced, contextual, culturally embodied, and unevenly held across roles, gender, and generations. The thesis identifies which aspects of local knowledge are represented in the DROP app and which are simplified or displaced when integrated into the interface. It also points to social and cultural shifts in norms, meaning, and values, influencing relationships and dynamics within forecasting networks and intergenerational knowledge transmission.

body.heading: Discussion & Contribution
body.text: The thesis discusses the implications of these findings for the design of the DROP app and, more broadly, for the future practice of climate services and service design. It surfaces benefits and limitations of both local and technical knowledge systems and argues for bridging these disciplines. Overall, the research invites practitioners to reflect more rigorously on the meaning of local knowledge integration and illustrates the complexities of designing with multiple knowledge systems. title: How can solar cooking be adapted to traditional Mayan food practices?
subtitle: Collaborating towards culturally grounded nutrition-energy transitions in rural Mexico

intro: Exploring how solar technologies can support everyday food practices while respecting local cultural meanings and daily routines.

body.heading: Purpose
body.text: The project investigates how sustainable cooking innovations can be made useful in the context of local food traditions. The challenge is to combine low-carbon energy transitions with social, practical, and cultural fit.

body.heading: Process & Methods
body.text: The research relied on household observation, cultural inquiry, prototype testing, and iterative redesign. The goal was to understand what makes a new cooking system acceptable, meaningful, and easy to integrate into daily life.

title: How can we navigate conflicting perspectives on the climate crisis?
subtitle: Playing with disagreement through dialogue, empathy and cooperation to reimagining collective futures

table.keywords: Games, conflict navigation, dialogue, climate communication

intro: Using game-based facilitation to explore disagreement and support constructive dialogue around climate-related challenges.

body.heading: Purpose
body.text: The project uses design games to create a safe and playful environment for discussing conflictive perspectives and building shared understanding.

body.heading: Process & Methods
body.text: The experience draws on facilitation design, role-play, and reflective co-creation to help participants navigate disagreement and identify common ground.
